row.Title: To amend the Permanent Electronic Duck Stamp Act of 2013 to allow States to issue electronic stamps under such Act, and for other purposes.
row.Summary: The bill amends the Permanent Electronic Duck Stamp Act of 2013 and related stamp statutes to let states issue electronic duck stamps and change how long those stamps remain valid. It replaces the prior 45-day limit with validity through the first June 30 after issuance and treats the electronic stamp as a permit under the Migratory Bird Hunting and Conservation Stamp Act. It also adds a requirement that states deliver an actual stamp after March 10 of each year to people who bought an electronic stamp during the prior 1-year period. State wildlife agencies gain a broader electronic sales option, and duck hunters gain immediate electronic permit access. Those same agencies must manage the later physical-stamp delivery requirement, and hunters must track the revised expiration and replacement timing.

row.Title: H.R. 5334 Engrossed Amendment Senate (EAS)
row.Summary: This bill is a sanctions measure addressing the Russian Federation and Iran rather than the tax deduction described in the official title, and the summarized Senate amendment text is dated August 7, 2026. It imposes sanctions on Russian officials, affiliated persons, vessels, and financial institutions, including the Central Bank of the Russian Federation, Sberbank, VTB Bank, and Gazprombank. It also bars new U.S. investment in Russia, restricts energy exports and imports tied to Russia, and raises duties on Russian goods and on goods from countries that keep buying Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas. Russian officials, banks, shipping interests, and energy firms lose access to U.S. property, visas, markets, and financing, while U.S. importers and investors face new trade and investment constraints. Ukrainian and humanitarian transactions receive limited exceptions, and the measure extends the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 to 2031 while setting the division to expire five years after enactment.

row.Title: To extend duty-free treatment provided with respect to imports from certain countries in Africa under the African Growth and Opportunity Act, to extend customs user fees, and for other purposes.
row.Summary: This bill extends duty-free treatment for certain imports from beneficiary sub-Saharan African countries under the African Growth and Opportunity Act and extends customs user fees, with key dates running through December 31, 2028 and December 31, 2031. It amends section 506B of the Trade Act of 1974 and section 112 of the African Growth and Opportunity Act to prolong preferential treatment, the regional apparel article program, and the third-country fabric program. It also authorizes retroactive liquidation or reliquidation of covered entries made after September 30, 2025 and before enactment, if a request is filed with U.S. Customs and Border Protection within 180 days. African exporters and apparel producers gain continued market access and possible refund treatment for covered entries, while importers and customs brokers must meet filing deadlines and documentation requirements. U.S. Customs and Border Protection must process additional reliquidation requests, and importers and consumers remain subject to extended customs user fees and merchandise processing fee dates through 2031.

row.Title: To amend title 38, United States Code, to make certain improvements relating to the eligibility of veterans to receive reimbursement for emergency treatment furnished through the Veterans Community Care program, and for other purposes.
row.Summary: The bill amends title 38 of the United States Code to change reimbursement rules for veterans’ emergency treatment through the Veterans Community Care program. It creates a 60-day window after enrollment during which prior receipt of care is not required for reimbursement. The measure leaves the change in place only for emergency treatment furnished on or after the date that is one year after enactment. row.Title: To amend the Federal Fire Prevention and Control Act of 1974 to authorize appropriations for the United States Fire Administration and firefighter assistance grant programs.
row.Summary: The bill authorizes appropriations for the United States Fire Administration and firefighter assistance grant programs, with a stated $95,000,000 annual authorization for the USFA for fiscal years 2024 through 2030. It also reauthorizes the Assistance to Firefighters Grants program by extending its sunset date to 2032 and its appropriations authority through 2030. A separate provision does the same for the Staffing for Adequate Fire and Emergency Response grant program, extending that sunset to 2032 and its appropriations authority through 2030. Fire departments and grant applicants gain continued access to USFA, Assistance to Firefighters, and SAFER funding, while the Comptroller General must produce two public GAO reports on barriers to accessing federal funds and on the US Fire Administration. The bill also excludes the Government of the People's Republic of China and China-based entities from receiving these fire grant funds, creating a new eligibility constraint for those organizations.

row.Title: S. 870 Engrossed Amendment House (EAH)
row.Summary: This measure authorizes and extends funding for the United States Fire Administration, firefighter assistance grants, the Fire Prevention and Safety Grants program, and the Staffing for Adequate Fire and Emergency Response grant program, while also revising multiple Nuclear Regulatory Commission and Department of Energy provisions. It sets the United States Fire Administration authorization at $95,000,000 annually for fiscal years 2024 through 2028, including $3,420,000 each year for section 8(f), and authorizes $750,000,000 annually for firefighter grant programs over the same period. It also creates an NRC International Nuclear Export and Innovation Branch, caps certain advanced reactor review fees, requires export and national-security notifications, and directs studies and reviews on global nuclear energy conditions and part 810 destinations. Fire departments, firefighter grant recipients, and the United States Fire Administration gain continued federal funding and longer program availability, while advanced reactor applicants, NRC staff, and export-focused nuclear entities receive new procedures and fee rules that shape their access and compliance obligations. Fire departments must contend with a GAO audit of funding barriers, nuclear applicants face fee caps and review sunsets, and companies handling covered fuel or qualifying exports must satisfy new consultation, notification, and licensing requirements.

row.Title: To authorize appropriations for the United States Fire Administration and firefighter assistance grant programs, to advance the benefits of nuclear energy, and for other purposes.
row.Summary: The act reauthorizes federal fire programs and advances nuclear energy policy through fiscal year 2028, while also extending some fire-program authorities to 2030. It sets the United States Fire Administration at $95,000,000 annually and reserves $3,420,000 each year for section 8(f) activities. It continues the Assistance to Firefighters Grants Program and the Fire Prevention and Safety Grants Program at $750,000,000 per year, extends SAFER, and requires a GAO audit of barriers to fire-department access to federal funds and of the United States Fire Administration. It also directs the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the Department of Energy, and the Department of State to expand international nuclear coordination, licensing review, advanced reactor prizes, and supply-chain and workforce studies. Fire departments, grant recipients, and advanced reactor developers gain continued funding and new licensing incentives, while NRC-regulated fuel owners, reactor applicants, and agency staff face new reporting, fee, security, and compliance requirements.
